conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally since your baby arrived. Everything you share stays confidential between you, me, and the clinical team, and there’s no right or wrong answer—just whatever feels true for you this past week. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can pause any time you need. Ready to begin?

Over the past seven days, how often have you found yourself able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly… not much at all. I’ll smile if someone makes a joke or if my husband tries to be silly, but it feels forced. Real laughter feels kind of out of reach—maybe once or twice I’ve actually chuckled, but even that fades fast.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… that’s what I mean—I can’t really say that. Most days nothing feels funny. I might give a little smile, but it’s like the joy is stuck behind a wall.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels flat. I’ll think “I should look forward to this,” but the feeling never shows up. Maybe once this week I sort of wanted to go out, but it faded before I even got dressed.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby won’t settle or I can’t get her to latch right, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong or I’m just not a good mom. Even when my partner says it’s normal, I still feel like I should be handling it better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s not breathing right, or I’ll lie awake imagining her choking in the crib. Nothing triggers it—it just lands on me and I can’t shake it for ages.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… it hits out of nowhere. Like yesterday, I was folding her tiny onesies and suddenly felt this wave—heart pounding, can’t catch my breath—like something awful is about to happen. I know nothing’s wrong, but my body feels like we’re in danger. It passes after a few minutes, but it keeps coming back.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It feels like I’m drowning in bottles, laundry, and her cries. I’ll start one thing, hear her fuss, drop it, then forget what I was doing. By suppertime I’m just staring at the mess, thinking I’ll never catch up. I manage to keep her fed and safe, but everything else feels too heavy.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning—reliving every little thing I might’ve done wrong, worrying she’ll wake up the second I drift off. It takes me over an hour to fall asleep most nights, and then I jolt awake at every tiny sound she makes.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… that’s most days. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll look at her tiny face and feel like I should be bursting with love, but mostly I just feel heavy and weepy. I cried in the shower yesterday and couldn’t really explain why.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A couple of times this week. Yesterday it was while I was rocking her—she finally settled and instead of feeling relieved I just started bawling. It’s like the sadness leaks out whether I want it to or not.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yeah… it’s crossed my mind, just a quick flash, maybe once or twice when everything feels too much. Like I’ll picture driving past the bridge and think “what if,” but I don’t want to die—I just want the pressure to stop. No plan, no real urge—just scary thoughts that pop in and scare me.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant age not specified)  
Date: [today]

Symptoms endorsed (EPDS‐10 paraphrase):  
- Joylessness, inability to laugh (Q1)  
- Marked anhedonia, anticipatory loss of pleasure (Q2)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame re parenting (Q3)  
- Daily free-floating anxiety, catastrophic worries about infant safety (Q4)  
- Recurrent panic-like surges without trigger (Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, unable to complete tasks (Q6)  
- Initial insomnia with intrusive rumination (Q7)  
- Persistent sadness, tearfulness (Q8, Q9)  
- Fleeting passive self-harm thoughts, no plan or intent (Q10)

Patterns: Consistent with moderate–severe depressive mood and comorbid postpartum anxiety; functional impairment noted in self-care, household tasks, and emotional bonding.

Screening significance / risk flags:  
- Positive for core depressive symptoms (low mood, anhedonia, guilt, tearfulness)  
- Postpartum anxiety symptoms exceed depressive items (panic attacks, safety obsessions)  
- Sleep disruption directly mood-linked  
- Passive suicidal ideation present → safety concern (low intent, no plan)  

Summary: Screening indicates high likelihood of postpartum major depressive episode with co-occurring anxiety; passive SI present. Recommend immediate formal psychiatric evaluation, safety planning, and consideration of specialized perinatal behavioral health services.
